description: We are a team of curious and creative problem-solvers passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration. We enjoy turning ideas into practical solutions and collaborating with people from different backgrounds. We welcome teammates with skills in programming, AI, data science, design, research, and creative thinking who are eager to learn and build something meaningful together.
summary:
Bara is an interactive web application that transforms over 25 years of NASA satellite hotspot data into an accessible fire activity calendar for Sarawak, Malaysia. It features interactive 2D and 3D maps, historical hotspot replay, seasonal comparisons, a rainfall-informed outlook, and Commander Mode, an educational simulation where users position fire trucks and test their decisions against actual historical hotspot patterns.
The project addresses the challenge of comparing MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations, which have different detection capabilities. By harmonizing older MODIS records to a VIIRS-equivalent scale, Bara creates a more consistent historical timeline for exploring burning activity, unusual conditions, and critical periods.
Starting with Mukah Division in Sarawak, Bara aims to make complex satellite information more meaningful for fire-response personnel, researchers, students, and local communities. Through scientific visualization and interactive learning, it encourages greater environmental awareness and a better understanding of historical fire patterns.
details:
What Exactly Does It Do?

Bara is an interactive web app that turns 25 years (2001 - 2026) of NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite hotspot records into one harmonized fire calendar for Sarawak, Malaysia, starting with Mukah Division. Its slogan sums up what it does :

• Watch: explore 25 years of burning patterns through a monthly calendar, 2D and 3D
maps and an animated replay.

• Warn: check a rainfall-informed outlook for next month’s hotspots.

• Protect: practise fire-truck dispatch in Commander Mode using real historical fire.


How Does Bara Work ?

1. Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS

MODIS and VIIRS see fires differently: VIIRS detects about 3 times more hotspots than MODIS. Without a fix, hotspot counts would seem to jump in 2012 only because a better satellite arrived, not because there was more burning. Using the years when both satellites overlap (2012 onward), Bara scales older MODIS counts onto a VIIRS-equivalent value, giving one fair timeline from 2001 to 2026 without double-counting.

We tested the method on 2025, a year it never saw: the yearly total came within 1% of the real count, while the older satellite alone would have counted 73% too few. Bara keeps an important difference clear: harmonized historical counts are estimates, while every hotspot location on the map is a real satellite observation.

2. Choose an Area, Dates and Series

Pick Sarawak, any division or any district, a date range between January 2001 and October 2026, and a month. Switch between the harmonized series and the raw MODIS or raw VIIRS counts at any time.

3. Historical Fire Calendar

A year-by-month grid from 2001 to 2026. Darker cells mean more hotspots. Pick any month, compare it with its normal seasonal level and spot unusually active periods.

4. Latest Month, In Plain English

For the selected month, Bara says how many hotspots satellites saw, whether that is higher or lower than normal, and what it means. A “Be prepared” box gives the local fire season and links to official air-quality readings (APIMS).

5. Interactive 2D and 3D Maps

The maps show real satellite hotspot locations, grouped into squares about 5 km wide. Click a district to zoom in. The 3D view uses columns (taller and darker means more hotspots) so concentrations stand out.

6. Historical Replay

Play 25 years of hotspots month by month at 1, 2 or 4 months per second. The map and calendar update together, so you can watch how activity changes over time.

7. Rainfall-informed Outlook

Bara estimates next month’s hotspots from past hotspot patterns and NASA POWER rainfall, with a likely range and dry / normal / wet rain scenarios. A month-by-month chart shows rain and hotspots together, with dry months highlighted.

The model was tuned on 2022–2024 and tested once on 2025. It is only shown where it beat a simple “typical month” guess; everywhere else Bara honestly shows the typical-month estimate and says so.

8. Commander Mode : Learn By Making Decisions

Pick a past month and place 5 fire trucks before the real hotspots are revealed. Bara then dispatches them: starting from the worst fire area, each of the 5 worst areas gets its nearest free truck, one truck per area, and the truck drives to that area’s busiest spot.

•      Main score: the average distance driven. Shorter trips mean a faster response.

•      Second score: how many hotspots were within 20 km of a truck.

•      Your plan is compared with the plan that covers the most hotspots, and a plain-
language “What happened” summary explains the result.

9. Open Data Downloads

Anyone can download the numbers as CSV files: monthly hotspots with rainfall, hotspot locations, and the next-month outlook.

What Benefits Does It Have ?

• Fire-response teams: see historical hotspot patterns and unusual periods, and
practise placing crews.

• Researchers and students: a consistent 25-year record that can be compared
fairly across the MODIS-to-VIIRS change.

• Local communities: clear, non-technical explanations of when and where burning
usually happens, plus preparedness tips.

• Children and young learners: satellite science and strategic thinking through
Commander Mode.

What Makes Bara Different ?

• Scientifically comparable data: MODIS and VIIRS harmonized into one timeline
without double-counting, and tested on a year the
method never saw.

• 25 years of interactive history: calendar, 3D maps and animated replay together.

• Honest outlook: the forecast is only shown where it proved better than a simple
guess.

• Learn through gameplay: Commander Mode turns real hotspot data into a dispatch
challenge.

• Plain Language for everyone: every panel explains what the numbers mean.

• Built for Sarawak: starting with Mukah Division, usable by professionals and the
public.

What Do We Hope To Achieve ?

We want satellite fire data to be understandable and useful for everyone in Sarawak, not only scientists, so people can prepare before the dry season instead of reacting to the haze. Next we would like to expand to all of Borneo and Southeast Asia, add NOAA-20/21 VIIRS, and refresh the data automatically each month.

Tools, Languages and Software

• Front end: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Python

• Visualization and animation: Three.js (3D maps), GSAP (animation)

• Data processing and modelling: Python, pandas, NumPy, Shapely, statsmodels
(Poisson / negative binomial regression), pyarrow,
requests, pytest

• Hosting and automation: GitHub, GitHub Actions and Netlify

• AI tools: Claude (Anthropic), Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot AI) and ChatGPT (OpenAI)
